title: Standard English verbs
keyIdea: Standard English is the form of English used in books, school writing and formal talk. Many people also speak a local form at home, such as we was or I done it; these are not mistakes in a chat, but school writing expects the Standard English verb. Use was with I, he, she, it and one person, and were with we, they, more than one and always with you (you were, even for one friend). did, saw, came and went stand on their own (I did it, I saw a fox); done, seen, come and gone need has, have or had in front (I have done it, she has seen it). ain't becomes isn't or aren't when it means be, and hasn't or haven't when it means have (I haven't got a pen).
familyTip: Play newsreader. Your child tells you about their day in their own words, then reads it again as a TV newsreader would, swapping any local forms (we was, I seen, she come) for Standard English (we were, I saw, she came). Keep it light: both ways of talking are real English, and a newsreader just picks the one everyone expects.

visual.caption: Was or were in Standard English? Drag each subject, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort was and were, choose did or done by the helper word, sort saw/seen pairs, swap ain't, fix a spoken recount, and pick when to use each.

kid: There is more than one way to speak English. At home you might say we was or I done it. In books and school writing we use Standard English: we were, I did it.
Use was with I, he, she, it and one person. Use were with we, they and more than one. You always takes were, even for one friend: you were right.
did stands on its own: I did my homework. done needs a helper word in front: I have done my homework. The same goes for saw and seen, came and come, went and gone. I saw a fox. I have seen a fox.
ain't is a local word. In Standard English say isn't or aren't for being, and hasn't or haven't for having. We aren't ready. I haven't got a pen.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. The national curriculum for England asks Year 4 pupils to use Standard English verb forms in place of local spoken forms. Its own examples are we were, not we was, and I did, not I done. The spoken language strand also asks pupils to use Standard English when the setting is formal.

Local forms such as we was, I seen, he come and ain't follow their own steady rules. They are not lazy speech. The aim is to add Standard English for writing and formal talk, not to correct a child's home voice. The key rule for the past is the helper word. The simple past (did, saw, came, went) stands alone. The past participle (done, seen, come, gone) comes after has, have or had.

Common mistakes: we was and you was (you takes were, even for one person); I done it and I seen it with no helper; overcorrecting to I have did or she has came; and picking the wrong word for ain't, such as they aren't got, when got shows it means haven't.

In the lab your child posts ten subjects to was or were. They drop did or done into six sentences where the helper is shown or missing. They sort ten past forms into stand alone and after a helper. They swap ain't in six sentences, tap the four local verbs in a spoken recount, and decide for six settings whether Standard English is expected.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is written in Standard English?
practice.hint: We means more than one person. Which past form goes with we?
practice.explain: We takes were: we were at the beach. We was is a local spoken form, and we is is the wrong tense and form.

practice.prompt: A story has {n} verbs. {k} of them are local forms like we was. How many verbs are already Standard English?
practice.hint: Take the local forms away from all the verbs.
practice.explain: {n} − {k} = {=n-k} verbs are already Standard English. The other {k} need swapping.

practice.prompt: Pick the Standard English: "I have ___ my jobs."
practice.hint: Is there a helper word, has, have or had, before the gap?
practice.explain: After have, use done: I have done my jobs. I have did is an overcorrection, and doed is not a word.

practice.prompt: Leo fixes {a} local verbs in his diary on Monday and {b} on Tuesday. How many does he fix in all?
practice.hint: Add Monday's fixes to Tuesday's fixes.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} verbs changed to Standard English, such as we was to we were.

practice.prompt: "She ain't here." How do you write it in Standard English?
practice.hint: Is this about being or having? She is one person.
practice.explain: Here ain't means is not, and she takes is: she isn't here. aren't is for we, you and they.

pool.prompt: Talking to one friend, which is Standard English?
pool.hint: you takes the same form for one person or many.
pool.explain: you always takes were, even for one person: you were brilliant. You was is a local form.

pool.prompt: Pick the Standard English: "I ___ a fox in the garden last night."
pool.hint: There is no has, have or had. Which form stands on its own?
pool.explain: With no helper, use saw: I saw a fox. seen needs a helper (I have seen), and have saw mixes the two.

pool.prompt: Which sentence about Dad is Standard English?
choices: Dad has came to get us.
pool.hint: This happened in the past with no helper word.
pool.explain: On its own, the past is came: Dad came to get us. After has, use come: Dad has come.

pool.prompt: "They ain't got time." Which is Standard English?
pool.hint: got tells you ain't means have here. Which have word goes with they?
pool.explain: got shows it means have, and they takes have: they haven't got time.

pool.hint: Which one is formal, for readers you do not know well?
pool.explain: A school report is formal writing, so Standard English is expected. In a chat at home, local forms are fine.

pool.prompt: Ali's recount has {a} local verbs in each of {p} paragraphs. How many verbs does he need to fix?
pool.explain: {a} × {p} = {=a*p} verbs to swap for Standard English.

pool.prompt: Pick the Standard English: "The children ___ tired after the trip."
pool.hint: The children means more than one. It happened in the past.
pool.explain: More than one takes were: the children were tired. was is for one person or thing.

pool.prompt: In a list of {n} verbs, {k} need has, have or had in front. How many can stand on their own?
pool.hint: Take away the ones that need a helper word.
pool.explain: {n} − {k} = {=n-k} verbs stand on their own, like did, saw and came.

pool.prompt: Pick the Standard English sentence about trying hard.
pool.hint: has is a helper word. Which form goes after it?
pool.explain: After has, use done: she has done her best. has did is an overcorrection, and she done has no helper.

pool.prompt: Which is a local spoken form, not Standard English?
pool.hint: Does seen have a helper word in front of it?
pool.explain: seen needs has, have or had in front. With no helper, Standard English says I saw it.
